data.title: Average Unemployment Duration Tops 27 Weeks, Long-Term Share Hits 27.6%
data.description: According to CNBC, the average period of unemployment exceeded 27 weeks in October, the longest outside the pandemic period since 2016, while about 2 million Americans had been jobless for at least 27 weeks. They made up 27.6% of all unemployed workers, the highest share since late 2021. Indeed senior economist Cory Stahle said the monthly data can fluctuate, but the longer-term trend is clear. The increase comes amid a low-hire, low-fire labor market, where employers are reluctant to lay off workers but are also adding few jobs. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond researchers wrote earlier this year that extended unemployment may reduce the likelihood of finding work as skills and professional networks erode and employers view long jobless spells negatively. Most workers can claim unemployment benefits for no more than 26 weeks in a year. Other October labor data showed nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 and the unemployment rate edged down to 4.1%. September job openings exceeded economists’ expectations, while layoffs and discharges fell to their lowest volume in more than a year.

data.title: OpenAI Bugging Suspect Abdulrahman Alfozan Pleads Not Guilty
data.description: According to CNBC, Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national charged with planting a listening device at OpenAI’s headquarters while working there, pleaded not guilty Friday in San Francisco federal court. He was sent back to jail after the hearing and has been held without bail since his arrest in early October.

data.title: Kazuo Ueda Says It Is Unclear How Long Japan Can Sustain 2% Inflation
data.description:
Japan’s inflation has reached policymakers’ 2% target, but Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said it is unclear how long that level can be maintained. According to Sina Finance, Ueda made the remarks during a question-and-answer session after a speech at the IMF on Friday, saying underlying inflation was at 2% and that the goal was to keep it there. He said it was unknown whether the current balance could be maintained for a long time, and that 2% inflation had not yet become fully established in Japanese society.

In a discussion with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Ueda gave no specific guidance on the central bank’s willingness to raise interest rates further. He described reaching the inflation target as an important milestone, but said more work remained and that appropriate monetary policy adjustments were needed to keep inflation at that level for years to come.

Earlier, Ueda spoke about the history of Japan’s current account surpluses and noted signs of renewed corporate risk appetite. He said bank lending growth had recently exceeded 5%, its fastest pace in 30 years, and that corporate risk appetite appeared to be recovering with the return of moderate inflation.

data.title: Canadian Dollar Faces Largest Weekly Decline Since September After Weak Jobs Data
data.description: The Canadian dollar is poised for its biggest weekly loss since late September after weaker-than-expected employment data reinforced concerns about the outlook for Canada’s economy, according to Bloomberg.

data.title: Microsoft Plans to Use Fewer Neoclouds as AI Buildout Shows Signs of Strain
data.description: According to CNBC, Microsoft plans to reduce its roster of neocloud partners and prioritize key suppliers and its own data centers. The company is evaluating its partnerships and has not decided which providers to drop, according to people familiar with the matter. Two sources said Microsoft chose not to renew a deal with Oracle.

data.title: FinCEN and Federal Reserve Withdraw $250 Cross-Border Crypto Transfer Proposal After Nearly 3,000 Comments
data.description:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the Federal Reserve Board withdrew a proposal to lower the information-collection threshold for certain cross-border crypto transfers from $3,000 to $250. According to Odaily, the agencies received nearly 3,000 comments, most opposing the lower threshold over concerns about compliance costs for smaller institutions and privacy risks from retaining more personal information.

The joint withdrawal notice was submitted on November 6 and is set to take effect on November 9. The agencies said they would seek public comment again before issuing a final rule if they pursue similar changes in the future.

The agencies also cited developments in the crypto industry and changes to the legal framework, including the payment stablecoin regulatory framework established by the GENIUS Act. The act took effect on July 18, 2025, establishing federal rules for payment stablecoin issuers.
